after: ## Issues in law and criminality at three levels
alt: Almost everyone agrees crime is bad, so that is not an issue. The disagreement is about what should be illegal, how offenders should be treated and who pays for prevention: globally, whether drug use is a crime or a health problem; nationally, the age of criminal responsibility; locally, youth clubs or extra patrols.
caption: Turn “crime” into a question about how to respond.

after: ## Issues in law and criminality at three levels
alt: Four purposes of punishment around a central sentence: deterrence, retribution, rehabilitation and restorative justice. Reoffending is how many judge a policy. Below, decriminalisation (still against the rules but not a criminal offence, possibly fined) is contrasted with legalisation (the act becomes lawful).
caption: Different views on crime often rest on different ideas of what punishment is for.

alt: A scale from 6 to 16 years marks the age of criminal responsibility: 10 in England and Wales; Scotland raised from 8 to 12 by its 2019 Act, in force from December 2021; and the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child encouraging at least 14 in General Comment No. 24 (2019).
caption: One issue shows national differences inside the UK and a global perspective from a UN body.

after: ## Perspectives: who thinks what, and why
alt: Portugal decriminalised personal possession and use of drugs in July 2001 under Law 30/2000, with panels referring people to treatment; trafficking stayed a crime, and other policy changes make effects hard to attribute. Around the question of treating drug use as a crime: a police officer (arrests deter), a doctor (records block treatment), a finance department (prison costs) and a bereaved parent (either view).
caption: Explain the reason behind each view before weighing them.

alt: A chain: a criminal record for a minor offence makes employers less willing to hire; without work or income the risk of reoffending may rise; the community pays again through more crime and court costs. Linking words such as because, so, which means that and as a result turn the steps into reasoning.
caption: Each link in the chain is a piece of reasoning to support with evidence.

alt: Bar chart for the fictional town of Harwell: recorded thefts on newly lit streets fell from 52 to 39 (25%), but in a nearby area with no new lights they fell from 48 to 38 (about 21%). Most of the fall may have happened anyway; a better test compares several lit and unlit streets over two years before and after, with a residents’ survey.
caption: A comparison area shows how much of a change would have happened anyway.

alt: Four traps in crime evidence: recorded crime is not all crime, so a rise can mean more crime, more reporting or new recording rules; fear of crime is not crime; correlation is not causation; and programmes may report only self-selected participants. A good suggested test names method, sample, comparison and measure.
caption: Ask what a crime figure actually measures before trusting it.

alt: Two actions on town-centre shoplifting placed on a timeline: police patrols give quick reassurance but do not address causes and may move crime elsewhere; a mentoring scheme targets a cause but takes longer and costs more per person. The judgement uses patrols briefly while mentoring is set up.
caption: Combine a quick action with one that tackles the cause.
